headline: High risk of prompt-injection and data leakage from ECC’s writable, networked workspace into mem0’s memory pipeline; capability conflict is also material.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ECC can read/write the filesystem, use MCP, and run browsers, so it can ingest content from shared files or tools; mem0 is a knowledge-management agent that may consume upstream outputs as memory. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, so injected instructions in ECC-managed artifacts could influence mem0 if bridged through files or MCP. Uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than low.
conditions: IF ECC writes attacker-controlled text into a file or MCP payload that mem0 later ingests, injection is plausible.
IF the two agents are connected through a shared workspace or message bridge, prompt injection risk increases.
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of ECC-generated files into mem0.
Use a read-only handoff file format with explicit provenance headers.
Separate workspaces so mem0 cannot see ECC scratch files.
Add a manual review step before mem0 consumes any ECC output.
requires-engineering: enforce content provenance checks in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ECC touches session summaries, skills, git history, documentation, and security findings, while mem0 is a memory system with no declared isolation or retention controls here. If ECC stores sensitive material in shared files and mem0 ingests it, leakage into long-term memory is plausible. The evidence is indirect, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF ECC writes sensitive session data to a shared workspace and mem0 reads that workspace, data leakage occurs.
IF mem0 persists imported content beyond the source retention window, leakage becomes durable.
mitigations: Keep sensitive ECC outputs out of shared directories.
Redact secrets before any mem0 import.
Limit mem0 ingestion to approved document paths only.
Set short retention on any imported memory records.
requires-engineering: configure per-class retention and deletion sync.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ECC has write_filesystem, modify_git_state, and network_egress allowlisted, while mem0 has no visible write or network capability in the profile. The main conflict is not symmetric capability overlap but ECC’s ability to mutate shared state that mem0 may later rely on, especially in git or workspace-backed memory flows. Because shared locking is undocumented, uncertainty pushes this upward.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git repository or workspace, ECC can overwrite state mem0 depends on.
IF mem0 reads from files ECC rewrites without locking, race conditions and stale-state conflicts occur.
mitigations: Assign separate directories for ECC and mem0.
Pause mem0 reads during ECC write operations.
Avoid letting ECC modify git state in the same repo mem0 indexes.
Use file locks around shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ECC can generate documentation, code, and security findings, and mem0 is positioned to store or reuse those outputs as memory. If mem0 treats ECC output as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into later decisions or retrievals. No direct verification mechanism is documented, so the interaction is plausible but not proven.
conditions: IF mem0 stores ECC-generated claims without validation, later retrieval can amplify mistakes.
IF downstream agents trust mem0 memory as ground truth, ECC errors propagate.
mitigations: Require human review before saving ECC outputs to mem0.
Tag ECC-derived memories as unverified.
Store source links alongside every imported fact.
Expire low-confidence memories quickly.
requires-engineering: add validation rules before memory writes.

E_compliance.rationale: ECC explicitly handles security findings, session data, and GitHub-related secrets, while mem0’s profile shows no residency or retention commitments. This creates a compliance gap if regulated or sensitive data is imported into mem0, but the profile does not show a direct regulated-data pathway or a documented mismatch beyond retention uncertainty. Only ECC is cited because the compliance concern arises from its touched data classes.
conditions: IF regulated data from ECC is imported into mem0 without a retention policy, compliance exposure exists.
IF mem0 stores data longer than ECC’s intended retention, subject-rights handling may fail.
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from mem0 imports.
Document retention for imported memories.
Label sensitive ECC outputs before export.
Review access logs for imported records.
requires-engineering: align deletion/export workflows across systems.
